Laguna bottlenose dolphins

Laguna, southern Brazil
cooperative foraging
Foraging

Dolphin populations off southern Brazil engage in cooperative foraging with artisanal fishermen: dolphins engage in circular movements to herd mullet shoals towards fishermen, then perform stereotyped movements, e.g. via head and tail slaps, to signal to the fisherman the time to cast their nets...

Recorded since 1847
Vertical: Inferred yesHorizontal: Inferred yesOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Dolphin populations off southern Brazil engage in cooperative foraging with artisanal fishermen: dolphins engage in circular movements to herd mullet shoals towards fishermen, then perform stereotyped movements, e.g. via head and tail slaps, to signal to the fisherman the time to cast their nets and the dolphins wait near the bottom to catch disoriented and escaping fish

Vertical: vertical: "The participation of the offspring in the interactions with artisanal fishery were followed in eight occasions, and were interpreted as learning sessions of hunting strategies" (Simões-Lopes et al. 1998)

Horizontal: cooperative foraging (or not) and home range were best predictors of dolphin social network associations. “Given that dolphins often copy and emulate their related and unrelated peers [8], social learning is likely to be involved in the spread and maintenance of the specialized foraging tactic among dolphins in Laguna [31]. When dolphins actively associate with few similar others, learning is facilitated within social modules rather than between modules [32]” (Machado et al. 2019)

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: Garland et al. (2025) categorize threats as 5.4 (Fishing & harvesting aquatic resources); 7.3 (Other ecosystem modifications); 9.1 (Domestic & urban waste water); 9.6 (Excess energy). Dolphins are not directly provisioned, and negative side effects such as reduced care for calves in provisioned Shark Bay dolphins not observed here. Although cooperative dolphins have a ~13% survival benefit (mark-recapture models), interactions have been declining, possibly due to mullet stock declines in southern Brazil due to overexploitation by regional and industrial fisheries (Cantor et al. 2023)

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Tramandaí bottlenose dolphins

Tramandaí, southern Brazil
cooperative foraging
Foraging

Dolphin populations off southern Brazil engage in cooperative foraging with artisanal fishermen: dolphins engage in circular movements to herd mullet shoals towards fishermen, then perform stereotyped movements, e.g. via head and tail slaps, to signal to the fisherman the time to cast their nets...

Vertical: Inferred yesHorizontal: Inferred yesOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Dolphin populations off southern Brazil engage in cooperative foraging with artisanal fishermen: dolphins engage in circular movements to herd mullet shoals towards fishermen, then perform stereotyped movements, e.g. via head and tail slaps, to signal to the fisherman the time to cast their nets and the dolphins wait near the bottom to catch disoriented and escaping fish

Vertical: vertical: "The participation of the offspring in the interactions with artisanal fishery were followed in eight occasions, and were interpreted as learning sessions of hunting strategies" (Simões-Lopes et al. 1998)

Horizontal: social network and homophily seem to play role in associations among cooperative fishers in Laguna

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: overfishing and risk to mullet stocks

Sources: [1] [3] [5]
site fidelity
Migration

Fidelity and use of site at Tramandaí Estuary. Year-to-year variability in area use, presence of some resident individuals who are at Tramandaí Estuary year-round as well as individuals who use it as part of larger range (Giacomo et al. 2017)

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Fidelity and use of site at Tramandaí Estuary. Year-to-year variability in area use, presence of some resident individuals who are at Tramandaí Estuary year-round as well as individuals who use it as part of larger range (Giacomo et al. 2017)

Domains: migration

Anthropogenic effects: "Additionally, the establishment of conservation measures in each estuary, as well as in adjacent regions, seems to be critical to guarantee the long-term persistence of these coastal units, as well as their unique foraging cooperation technique with artisanal fishermen" (Giacomo et al. 2017)

Sources: [4]

Social unit: Group. "Groups of Common Bottlenose Dolphins most often consist of 2 - 15 individuals, although groups of more than 1000 individuals have been reported. Group structure varies greatly with factors such as sex, age, reproductive status, and kinship." [6]
